title: Updating working memory in aircraft noise and speech noise causes different fMRI activations
research_question: To investigate how visual-verbal working memory is updated when exposed to three different background-noise conditions (speech noise, aircraft noise, and silence) using fMRI/BOLD neuroimaging, and to study the neural underpinnings of updating processes in the presence of these noise sources.

participants.description: 8 males and 10 females, healthy, right-handed adults with a mean age of 24.3 years (ranging from 20 to 28), reported to be of normal hearing and to have Norwegian as their native language.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Aircraft noise (recorded near an airport), speech noise (Norwegian male actor reading a meaningful, structured, fictitious story with non-salient content). Both sounds were digitalised, edited to 40 seconds duration, made equivalent in volume, and played back in mono at approximately 70 dB(A) SPL. A silence condition was also used.

Double-digit numbers (15-99) presented as white text on a black background, in Arial type and font size 72, on MRI-compatible glasses (600 x 800 pixel resolution). 12 lists of 10 numbers each were used.

measures.construct: Neural activation during working memory updating
measures.instrument: fMRI/BOLD neuroimaging (3.0T GE Tesla Signa Excite MRI scanner, T1-weighted MPRAGE, 336 BOLD-sensitive echo-planar image (EPI) volumes, TR=3s, 25 slices, 64x64 voxel matrix, 3x3x5mm cubic voxels)

measures.construct: Behavioral accuracy in working memory updating task
measures.instrument: Response clicker (thumb/index finger button for 'substitution' or 'no substitution')

findings.quote: The participants' performance on responses indicating whether or not they updated their WM content had a high accuracy across trial types (overall accuracy, M = 95%, SD = 21.7%).

findings.antecedent: Background noise condition (silence, speech noise, aircraft noise)
findings.consequent: Behavioral accuracy in working memory updating task
findings.mechanism: Participants may have increased mental effort to compensate for interference, leading to comparable behavioral performance despite different neural activations.
findings.quote: The response accuracy rates were comparable between the conditions... and t-test comparisons were not significantly different (all p > 0.5).

findings.antecedent: Substitution processes (adding new items, suppressing old) in working memory updating task
findings.consequent: Neural activation in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), posterior medial frontal cortex, and parietal lobes
findings.mechanism: Associated with cognitive conflict detection and the 'manipulation/change' network for WM representation.
findings.quote: The DLPFC, the posterior medial frontal cortex and the parietal lobes were activated more by 'substitution' trials...

findings.antecedent: Exclusion processes (rejecting new items, maintaining intact memory) in working memory updating task
findings.consequent: Neural activation in anterior medial frontal cortex
findings.mechanism: Associated with excluding potentially, but not currently, relevant stimuli and cognitive conflict detection.
findings.quote: the anterior medial frontal cortex was more activated by 'no substitution' trials...

findings.antecedent: Performing task with speech noise (vs. silence)
findings.consequent: Neural activation in bilateral temporal cortex (left and right superior temporal gyrus)
findings.quote: doing the task with speech as a background noise... activated the bilateral but left-lateralized temporal cortex...

findings.antecedent: Performing task with aircraft noise (vs. silence)
findings.consequent: Neural activation in left temporal cortex (left superior temporal gyrus)
findings.quote: Doing the task with aircraft noise as a background noise... activated only the left temporal cortex...

findings.antecedent: Speech noise (vs. aircraft noise) during task
findings.consequent: Neural activation in left middle temporal gyrus and anterior cingulum
findings.mechanism: Semantic referents in speech may automatically activate cognitive processes, leading to cognitive conflict and increased demand for cognitive control to concentrate on the intended signal.
findings.quote: a subtraction between the two noises showed an area in the left temporal lobe to be more activated by speech than by aircraft noise...

findings.antecedent: Aircraft noise (vs. speech noise) during task
findings.consequent: Neural activation in right postcentral gyrus, right supramarginal gyrus, and right cerebellum 6
findings.mechanism: Sub-threshold effects, possibly related to differences in acoustic characteristics (frequency distribution) between noise types.
findings.quote: aircraft noise did not activate any areas more than speech did at the chosen alpha levels. Reducing the alpha level to p < 0.05 to explore sub-threshold effects revealed activation in the basal structures of the right temporal lobe and cerebellum (contrast 6).

findings.antecedent: Substitution processes in speech noise (vs. aircraft noise)
findings.consequent: Neural activation in medial PFC (middle cingulate, supplemental motor area), right precentral gyrus, and right postcentral gyrus
findings.mechanism: Greater medial PFC activity suggests increased cognitive control and active inhibition needed to exclude task-irrelevant speech content from WM.
findings.quote: trials requiring updating processes undertaken with speech in the background are associated with a greater activation in the medial PFC... than substitution trials undertaken with aircraft noise...

findings.antecedent: Substitution processes in aircraft noise (vs. speech noise)
findings.consequent: Neural activation in occipital, parietal, and frontal cortex (e.g., left inferior parietal gyrus, right superior parietal gyrus, left superior frontal gyrus)
findings.mechanism: Increased reliance on visual imagery/visuo-spatial sketchpad to perform the task, possibly due to speech noise interfering more with the phonological loop.
findings.quote: 'substitution' trials with aircraft noise in the background... activated the occipital, parietal and frontal cortex...

mechanisms: Cognitive conflict detection (anterior prefrontal cortex for 'no substitution' trials, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex for 'substitution' trials)
Exclusion of task-irrelevant stimuli from working memory
Auditory processing of background noise (temporal lobes)
Increased cognitive control and active inhibition due to semantic content in speech noise
Cross-modal compensation: increased reliance on visual imagery/visuo-spatial sketchpad when phonological loop is interfered with by speech noise.
implementation_implications: Differences in noise types (e.g., speech vs. aircraft) can affect higher-order cognitive capabilities like reading comprehension and prose memory differently.
Verbal distractors during verbal tasks require additional cognitive control.
Noise-induced impairment of cognitive control, specifically WM updating processes, may explain the deteriorating effect of noise on reading comprehension.

tables.description: Clusters of voxels significantly more activated in the contrasts of interest, showing t-threshold, cluster size, MNI coordinates (X, Y, Z), t-value, z-value, anatomical localization, and Brodmann area for 8 fMRI contrasts.
key_stats: t-thresholds: 7.154 (familywise error corrected, p < 0.05), 3.965 (uncorrected, p < 0.0005), 1.74 (uncorrected, p < 0.05)

limitations: The scanner environment did not allow participants to report their actual memory content, relying on task performance and fMRI analyses to infer memory operations.

Behavioral performance (accuracy) did not differ significantly across noise conditions, suggesting fMRI differences reflect different cognitive mechanisms or degrees of involvement rather than performance decrements.
Differences in activation caused by the sounds themselves (regardless of the task) may be partly due to differences in frequency distribution between the two types of sound.

paper_metadata.title: Updating working memory in aircraft noise and speech noise causes different fMRI activations
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Updating working memory in aircraft noise and speech noise causes different <scp>fMRI</scp> activations
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The present study used fMRI/BOLD neuroimaging to investigate how visual‐verbal working memory is updated when exposed to three different background‐noise conditions: speech noise, aircraft noise and silence. The number‐updating task that was used can distinguish between “substitution processes,” which involve adding new items to the working memory representation and suppressing old items, and “exclusion processes,” which involve rejecting new items and maintaining an intact memory set. The current findings supported the findings of a previous study by showing that substitution activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the posterior medial frontal cortex and the parietal lobes, whereas exclusion activated the anterior medial frontal cortex. Moreover, the prefrontal cortex was activated more by substitution processes when exposed to background speech than when exposed to aircraft noise. These results indicate that (a) the prefrontal cortex plays a special role when task‐irrelevant materials should be denied access to working memory and (b) that, when compensating for different types of noise, either different cognitive mechanisms are involved or those cognitive mechanisms that are involved are involved to different degrees.
